lesson.guided_practice:
WE DO — attempt each prompt before comparing to the feedback.
1. Put these events in sensible order: We dried the dog; the dog jumped in a puddle; we went home.
COMPARE: The dog jumped in a puddle. We went home. We dried the dog. Drying follows getting wet.
2. Improve the opening "He ran away" by naming the character, place and reason for moving.
COMPARE: One option: "At the school oval, Ben ran towards the gate to catch his rolling ball." It answers who, where and why.
3. Shorten "Then the gardener found the missing bucket beside the tree" into three or four note words.
COMPARE: "gardener / bucket / beside tree" preserves the important detail; full grammar is not required in notes.
4. Read these notes aloud as a two-sentence story: rain—path / sister—umbrella. Add a pause between events.
COMPARE: "Rain soaked the path. My sister opened her umbrella." Pause naturally after the first complete thought.
lesson.independent_task:
YOU DO — complete the following substantial original task, not a copied model.
Plan a real or invented four-event story about an unexpected visitor. Make four brief cue lines (not full sentences), tell the story in four or five complete spoken sentences, then record which cue helped most and one improvement you made after rehearsing. Write or record the final version.

teach_steps.example:
WATCH MY THINKING
I tell a short story about losing my hat: First I put it on near the oval. Next the wind carried it over the fence. Then the groundskeeper returned it. Finally I thanked her. Each event leads naturally to the next.

YOUR SMALL TRY
Put these events in sensible order: We dried the dog; the dog jumped in a puddle; we went home.

COMPARE AND CORRECT
The dog jumped in a puddle. We went home. We dried the dog. Drying follows getting wet.
teach_steps.explain:
A listener needs to know what happened first, next and at the end. Temporal words signal changes, but events must also connect logically.

A listener needs to know what happened first, next and at the end. Temporal words signal changes, but events must also connect logically. This matters because a reader or listener can only understand your ideas when you notice how the language works, test your understanding on specific examples and explain the evidence for your choice. Keep the meaning of the original text rather than changing facts to make an answer sound impressive. Read the model closely: which particular word, event or detail changes the meaning? Try explaining the same decision to someone else without repeating the model sentence. Then compare your new attempt with the feedback and revise anything that does not fit the actual evidence.
teach_steps.notice:
WATCH OUT
Do not assume saying finally makes an event a logical ending. Re-read the prompt and correct the misunderstanding before moving on.

I tell the hat story, pause after the wind blows, and ask "Could you tell where the hat went?" If the listener asks which fence, I add "the fence beside the tennis court".

lesson.title: Year 3: Tell a story and prepare readable notes
lesson.worked_example:
I DO — I tell a short story about losing my hat: First I put it on near the oval. Next the wind carried it over the fence. Then the groundskeeper returned it. Finally I thanked her. Each event leads naturally to the next.

Now look for the exact evidence in the words or actions. Instead of starting "It went missing", I begin "On Saturday, Zara left her red kite beside the beach path." Now a listener can picture Zara, the kite and the location.
